description: warden reads a new Pons v2 launch on-chain in one multicall and extracts risk signals (LP lock, mint/blacklist functions, ownership renounce, holder concentration, dev-buy size)
steps: Point warden at a Pons v2 token address
Run `warden scan <address>`

Verify it returns LP-lock status, mint/blacklist/deployer-privilege facts, top-holder concentration %, and dev-buy size and count, combining live per-token reads (curve state, LP lock, holders, dev-buy history) with fixed facts confirmed once from the token template's source (no mint/blacklist function exists in PonsV2LauncherToken.sol for any Pons v2 launch)

description: warden fingerprints a launch's linked GitHub repo (if any) for authenticity red flags: account-age-vs-activity mismatch, fork/star bursts clustered in a tight time window, self-promoted token ticker in README or author bio
steps: Point warden at a launch that links a GitHub repo
Run `warden vet-repo <owner>/<repo>`

Verify it reports account creation date vs the account's oldest visible repo (a proxy for first activity), fork creation timestamps and whether they cluster within a 30-minute window, and separately reports raw contract-address mentions (weak signal, common in legitimate protocol docs) vs $TICKER mentions (much sharper signal) found in the README/bio. Star-burst timing is out of scope: GitHub restricted stargazer-listing for third-party repos in July 2026, and this must be surfaced as unavailable, never silently treated as zero.

Verify against a known-bad repo (github.com/Phosphenq/bodkin, profiled in this project's own research: 2019 account dormant until 2026-09-03, 6 forks in a 19-minute window, $BODKIN in both README and bio) that the tool reproduces that exact profile, and against a known-legitimate repo (github.com/ponsdotdev/ponsfamily) that it does NOT flag its legitimate contract-address mentions as ticker-shilling

description: an LLM agent combines the on-chain read and the repo fingerprint into a plain-language verdict with a reasoning log, not just a score
steps: Run `warden judge <address> [--repo <owner>/<repo>]` on a launch with on-chain data (and optionally repo fingerprint data) available
Verify the output is a written verdict (not just a number) that cites the specific signals it weighed, each tied to a real field/value from the input, not a vague claim
Verify a reasoning log is saved alongside the verdict (verdicts/<token>-<timestamp>.json)

BLOCKED on live verification: this environment has no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (checked, not set, and the Claude Code session's own credentials are a separate thing not to be smuggled in here). Implementation is done, wired end-to-end through the real scan+vet-repo pipeline, and fails cleanly with an actionable error at the API-key gate (verified live against a real launch) - but the actual model call, its output shape, and whether it follows the system prompt's rules have NOT been exercised. Add a real key to .env and re-run before flipping this to true.

description: warden pushes each verdict to a Telegram chat in real time as new launches are scanned
steps: Configure a Telegram bot token and chat id
Run `warden watch` (live feed - polls the real factory) or `warden watch --once <token>` (test feed - one already-known launch, no waiting)
Verify a message with the verdict and key signals arrives in the configured Telegram chat

BLOCKED on live verification, same shape of gap as the judge feature: no TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN/TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID exist for this project yet. What IS verified live: the full watch loop polling real chain state and finding real launches (a live regression run surfaced two real bugs, both now fixed - see claude-progress.txt for the empty-string --once bug and the public-RPC rate-limit-under-sustained-polling finding), sendTelegramAlert failing cleanly and specifically without credentials, and formatVerdictMessage's output shape (unit tested). Never actually delivered a message. Create a real bot via @BotFather, add its token + your chat id to .env, and re-run before flipping this to true.

description: warden defaults to dry-run (alert-only, no trade execution) and requires an explicit --live flag plus a verdict-confidence threshold before it will submit any transaction
steps: Run `warden watch` without --live: verify no transaction is ever submitted, only alerts

Run `warden watch --live --min-confidence 0.8 --buy-amount-eth <n>`: verify a transaction is only submitted when the verdict is low_risk AND confidence clears the threshold AND the launch is paired with native ETH (not an ERC20 - only that path is implemented), and that every decision - attempted or not - is logged (verdicts/trades.jsonl) with the verdict that triggered it

Verify the slippage-protected minTokensOut this project computes off-chain (src/execute/quote.ts) matches what the real curve contract itself computes, via a live eth_call simulation - not by trusting the formula was transcribed correctly

DELIBERATELY NOT LIVE-TESTED beyond simulation: this is the one feature that can move real money, and this project's own standing rule (do not fund a wallet or broadcast a real transaction to verify a feature) means passes stays false regardless of how solid the gate logic and simulation results are. What IS verified, live: the exact buy(uint256,uint256,address) signature (read from real source, not guessed), the off-chain slippage-floor math is BIT-FOR-BIT identical to a real curve's own simulateContract result (0 bps difference, cross-checked live), the safety gate itself has 7 passing unit tests covering every combination of verdict/confidence/pair-type/--live, and a live end-to-end run of `watch --once <token> --live` correctly printed the --live warning banner and still failed cleanly at an earlier, unrelated gate (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) - proving --live doesn't bypass any upstream check. A live buy-simulation against a real launch also surfaced a real gap this project didn't know it had: some launches are paired with an ERC20 quote token, not native ETH (~30% in one sample) - only the native path is implemented, and the gate explicitly refuses (not silently mishandles) the ERC20 case.

description: warden supports more than one launchpad (Pons v2 first, extensible adapter interface for others)
steps: Add a second launchpad adapter implementing the same interface as the Pons v2 reader: done for four.meme on BNB Smart Chain (src/chain/fourmeme.ts), a real, currently-active bonding-curve launchpad picked specifically for having a genuinely different LP-lock mechanism (burns LP via a DEX pair, no locker contract) and owner-privilege model (the manager legitimately holds Ownable control pre-graduation, unlike Pons's always-zero-privilege deployer) - chosen to stress-test the interface, not to duplicate Pons with different addresses

Run `warden scan <token> --launchpad four-meme`: verified against multiple real live launches (one native-BNB-paired, one ERC20-quoted - the same pairToken lesson from Pons applies here independently)

Verify identical output shape to the Pons v2 path via `--normalized` on both: confirmed both by field-by-field inspection and by an automated test (src/chain/launchpad.test.ts) that runs both adapters against real live launches and diffs Object.keys() directly, including the ownerPrivilege sub-shape. The two protocols' normalized `ownerPrivilege.active` values genuinely differ (false for Pons, true for four.meme pre-graduation) - that's the interface correctly carrying real protocol differences, not a bug to reconcile away.

Contract addresses/signatures were independently re-verified live in this project (eth_call/eth_getCode/eth_getStorageAt), not taken on trust from the community doc that first named them, including catching and correcting a wrong assumed proxy storage slot before it was ever encoded - see claude-progress.txt for the full trail. 12 new tests, all passing, all against live chain state (BSC + a specific known graduated pair for the burn-arithmetic check, since this session's own RPC hit eth_getLogs query-limit errors trying to self-discover a graduated example - the PancakeSwap-wide log volume on BSC is too high for a public RPC's window, documented honestly rather than silently working around it).

description: warden ships a backtest mode that replays historical launches through the scoring pipeline and reports an honest win-rate, so any claimed accuracy is self-provable rather than a self-reported claim
steps: Run `warden backtest --since <date>`

Verify it replays real historical launches (not synthetic data) through the same scan+judge pipeline: src/backtest/discover.ts finds real TokenLaunched events chunked backward from latest (the factory's activity level can exceed a single eth_getLogs call's result limit over a wide range, learned earlier in this project), each one is fed through the real scanLaunch and judgeLaunch

Scope correction from the original wording: does NOT report 'actually rugged' - that needs a stronger evidentiary bar (price history, holder-exit patterns) than this project can defend, and Pons's own design already structurally blocks the classic rug vectors (vault-locked LP, zero deployer privilege) this project could check for. Reports the honest, objectively-checkable alternative instead: graduated vs. abandoned (stalled, never graduated) vs. active vs. too-recent-to-call, each with its own on-chain evidence string, cross-tabulated against judge's verdict category. summarizeBacktest never fabricates a count for an entry whose verdict is unavailable - unit-tested directly.

BLOCKED on live verification for the judge portion, same as features 2/3: no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in this environment, so every judgeLaunch call inside the backtest loop fails (gracefully - verdictError is recorded per-entry, the loop continues, the rest of the pipeline still runs). What IS verified: the historical-launch discovery logic and the outcome-classification logic both have passing tests (4 for classifyOutcome, 2 for summarizeBacktest, all pure-logic and fully verified; 1 live-network test for findHistoricalLaunches against a real recent window, though this specific run hit the same already-documented cumulative rate limit from this session's own heavy testing load - the identical getContractEvents pattern this test uses was independently confirmed working many times earlier in this session, e.g. in pons.test.ts and watch.test.ts, before that limit set in).
